newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Pyongyang defector sparks political storm in Seoul.
newsitem.headline: Pyongyang defector sparks political storm in Seoul.

text.p: The script could have been written by South Korea's spymasters: a top Pyongyang defector warns of nuclear attack, links North Korean leader Kim Jong-il to Hitler, calls his country "one big prison" and advocates harsh deterrence.
Indeed, some think it was.

So closely do comments made by Hwang Jang-yop, the highest-ranked official ever to flee North Korea, mirror the hawkish line of the security agencies that some civic groups and politicians are crying foul.
A Red Scare threatens to poison the atmosphere as South Korea and the United States try to coax Pyongyang to accept peace talks.
It also plays into the hands of the ruling New Korea Party in a presidential election year.
The main opposition leader, Kim Dae-jung, has long been tainted by suspicions he harbours pro-Pyongyang sympathies.

"For the present, there is little reason to doubt his word and his motives for defecting," said an editorial in the Korea Times, referring to Hwang's self-proclaimed mission as an ambassador for peace.
"Yet, we must caution that his defection could trigger a new source of confrontation between the two Koreas."
Pyongyang's reaction to Hwang's arrival in Seoul on Sunday has been uncharacteristically restrained. State-run radio made a mild jab at an unnamed "cowardly traitor".
Instead, Hwang's barbs seem to be creating more of a stir in South Korea.

Among other revelations in a document attributed to him by the Chosun Ilbo daily, Hwang said North Korea could turn South Korea into a "sea of flames" and scorch Japan in a nuclear and chemical attack.
Kim Jong-il "worshipped Hitler", had a hot temper and was "capricious and jealous of everyone".
Any outside investment in North Korea would go straight into the pockets of the military, Hwang argued. Send food aid to help alleviate starvation, he advised, but not too much.
Calculations about Kim's personality and state of mind, North Korea's fire-power and the role of the military help shape South Korean and U.S. approaches towards the secretive country.
Washington's policy of "cautious engagement" supposes that Pyongyang can be drawn out of isolation, and that ultimately it might be persuaded to make peace.
Not so, according to Hwang, whose loudest message has been that Pyongyang is bent on destruction of its neighbour.
"South Korea must create a society that respects the military and strengthens national defences to prepare to win any war," the Chosun Ilbo document said.

Hardliners in both South Korea and Pyongyang oppose any conciliation between the two Koreas -- still technically at war since their 1950-53 conflict ended only in a truce -- and would be happy to see a tentative peace process derailed.

Although Seoul officials see no direct link, Hwang's arrival in South Korea coincided with the collapse of talks in New York between the two Koreas and the United States designed to entice Pyongyang to peace negotiations.
In a harshly-worded statement, a Roman Catholic group scoffed at Hwang's assertions that his mission was to promote inter-Korean peace.
"A cow would laugh at that," said the Roman Catholic Priests Association for Justice.
"You know the North Korean communist party better. We know the South Korean intelligence agency better," the priests said, accusing Hwang of being a dupe.
Among those benefiting from Hwang is President Kim Young-sam, whose term in office expires next February.
Hwang's sensational warnings of impending war have grabbed the headlines away from Kim and a corruption scandal engulfing the final year of his presidency.

The Agency for National Security Planning -- the domestic intelligence body now sheltering Hwang -- is clearly worried by suspicions it is playing puppet-master. It issued a rebuttal to media reports suggesting it had scripted the defector's statements.
Newspapers digging into the language had noted several phrases with an oddly South Korean flavour coming from the mouth of a Pyongyang communist party apparatchik.
